title: Integral
body:
Integration is the other half of the course, and it comes in two flavours that look alike, mean
different things, and are connected by the [[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus]].

| | Notation | What it is | Answer is |
|---|---|---|---|
| **indefinite** | $\int f(x)\,dx$ | the family of antiderivatives of $f$ | a **function** (plus $C$) |
| **definite** | $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ | the signed area under $f$ from $a$ to $b$ | a **number** |

> The indefinite integral needs $+C$ and the definite integral must not have one. Losing the $+C$
> is the most common mark dropped in the course, and it is not pedantry: two functions with the
> same [[Derivative]] differ by a constant, and by the [[Mean Value Theorem]] that constant is the
> *only* thing the derivative cannot see.

## Antiderivatives

An antiderivative of $f$ is any $F$ with $F' = f$. Reversing differentiation is a matter of reading
the [[Differentiation Rules]] tables right to left:

$$
\int x^n\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \quad (n \neq -1), \qquad \int \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln|x| + C
$$
$$
\int e^x dx = e^x + C, \qquad \int \cos x\,dx = \sin x + C, \qquad \int \sin x\,dx = -\cos x + C
$$

The $n = -1$ exception is not a special case bolted on; it is where the power rule would divide by
zero, and $\ln$ is exactly the function that fills the hole. The absolute value in $\ln|x|$ matters
because $1/x$ is defined for negative $x$ too.

**There is no product rule, quotient rule, or chain rule for integration.** Differentiation is
mechanical and always succeeds on elementary functions; integration is a pattern-matching search
that can fail. $\int e^{-x^2}dx$ has no elementary antiderivative at all, which is precisely why
the normal distribution's CDF in [[STATISTICS]] is read from a table instead of computed.

## The definite integral

$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ is defined as a limit of [[Riemann Sum|Riemann sums]]: chop $[a,b]$ into $n$
strips, approximate each by a rectangle, add them up, let $n \to \infty$. That definition is what
the integral *is*; the [[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus]] is the shortcut that makes it
computable.

The area is **signed**. Regions below the axis count negative, so $\int_{-1}^{1} x\,dx = 0$ even
though the picture obviously has area in it. For total geometric area you split at the roots and
integrate $|f|$ piecewise.

Useful properties, all obvious from the area picture:

- $\int_a^a f = 0$, and $\int_b^a f = -\int_a^b f$
- $\int_a^c f = \int_a^b f + \int_b^c f$
- linearity: constants pull out, sums split

## What it is for

- **Accumulation.** If $f$ is a rate, $\int_a^b f$ is the total accumulated between $a$ and $b$.
  Integrate velocity, get displacement. This is the reading that generalises furthest.
- **Probability.** A [[Probability Density Function]] is a function whose integral over the whole
  line is $1$. A probability is an area under it, the CDF is its antiderivative, and
  $E[X] = \int x f(x)\,dx$ is [[Average Value]] with the sum of a discrete mean replaced by an
  integral. This is why [[CALCULUS 1]] is the stated prerequisite for [[STATISTICS]].
- **Averages.** The mean value of $f$ on $[a,b]$ is $\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f$, which is "add up the
  values and divide by how many" with the sum and the count both taken to a continuum.

## Technique

[[U-Substitution]] is the only one Calc 1 teaches. [[Integration Techniques]] in [[CALCULUS 2]]
picks up parts, partial fractions, and trigonometric substitution, and the [[Double Integral]]
extends the area picture to volumes on the way into [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]].
